items_missed: No agenda statement and no 'sound good?'. The closest was 'I just kind of doing my general proving questions' — which names the activity but gives no roadmap, no timeframe, and no confirmation ask. On a sixteen-minute call that ended up restructuring the customer's entire move into two jobs across two days, previewing the shape of the conversation would have saved several of the dead-air stretches.

Stairs and floors never asked at either location. Not at the origin house, not at the Norwood Cove destination. The customer eventually volunteered the gap herself — 'there are a few pieces already in the garage, at the new house where we could have them like, carry those up to their final destinations as well' — the word 'up' is doing a lot of work there and nobody followed it. On a six-hour estimate, whether the destination has stairs is not a detail.

Additional rooms never asked. The customer volunteered the garage twice ('we've already moved a chunk of stuff into the garage of the new place') and it was never probed as a room with contents, a staging area, or a destination.
Special considerations never asked — no long walks, no narrow hallways, no tight turns, at any of three locations including a commercial furniture warehouse the crew has never been to.

Box count never asked. This is a three-bedroom, roughly 1,000-square-foot house with a family packing around a due date, and nobody established how many boxes exist. It is the largest single input into a six-hour estimate and it was never collected.

Packing needs never asked — no packing-service offer on a household where the customer is thirty-seven weeks pregnant and openly described the situation as 'a little bit hectic in our lives at the moment.' That is the clearest packing upsell signal in this week's sample and it went unoffered.

Access concerns never asked at any of the three stops. No parking question, no gate, no HOA, no loading dock or receiving procedure at the Four Hands warehouse — a commercial vendor location with its own pickup process that the customer herself was unsure about.

The moving-stressor question was never asked, despite the customer handing over the answer unprompted: 'we're at the new house as they work on these bathrooms, we're trying to get moved in here obviously, on this timeline because I have a baby doing three weeks. So just trying to make sure... It's a little bit hectic in our lives at the moment.' Hector responded warmly and personally — 'Wow, congratulations' — but never converted any of it into a logistics question. An active bathroom renovation at the destination on move day is a real access constraint and it was heard as small talk.

What's-included was never stated. No gas, no truck, no taxes, no insurance, no wrap, pads, or bands. Only the tools for disassembly were named as included. The customer heard a $222 hourly rate with almost nothing attached to it.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned — on a three-stop move that includes picking up brand-new furniture directly from a manufacturer's warehouse. If a new Four Hands console is damaged between the warehouse and Norwood Cove, the customer has no idea what Einstein does about it.

Meet Your Mover never mentioned. Two different crews are coming to this customer's home on two consecutive days while she is late in a pregnancy and living in a house under renovation. Naming and putting faces to the crews in advance is built for exactly this.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned, despite the entire call turning on arrival windows — a 12:30 Saturday slot the customer accepted, and a Friday slot negotiated from 1:30 to 12:00 to 2:30.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener and no hidden-fees pitch. The trip-fee reassurance was handled well but the broader no-credit-card-fee / no-fuel-surcharge / no-assembly-fee claim was never made.

The clock explanation never said when the clock starts. The minimum and the fifteen-minute proration both landed, but billable time's starting trigger was never stated — on a two-day job with a warehouse pickup where the customer has every reason to wonder whether the drive between stops is on her clock.
No sense-check anywhere. The customer supplied her own — 'So if we, if we come in under then we reduce awesome' — which Hector confirmed, but he never asked.
No typical time range for the home size. The six hours was inherited from Arden's original estimate and asserted, never benchmarked against what a three-bedroom normally runs.
Truck count never stated. The customer was told 'the two mover expectation' and never heard how many trucks, across a job that now involves two separate crews on two days.
Walk distance never asked anywhere — origin, destination, or warehouse.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors used at any point.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10. The customer had already done the work and said so: 'we've already moved a chunk of stuff into the garage of the new place' and later 'We'll try to, we'll try to make the best use of that time as possible.' She was doing his job for him. The response went the opposite direction — 'the movers are definitely look for opportunities to help out too' — which is about filling the two-hour minimum, not about shortening the six-hour day. No prep-saves-money framing, no consolidation examples, no carload tip, no close.

No confirmation email was ever offered. This is the most serious miss on the call. Hector booked two separate jobs on two different days, moved the Saturday start from 8:30 to 12:30, negotiated the Friday start from 1:30 to 2:30, cut the Friday minimum from 2.5 hours to 2.0, restructured which crew does the assembly, and produced a new combined total of $1,776 — and never said he would put any of it in writing. There is no email, no bolded detail list, no 'reply with any corrections.' Everything material that changed on this call exists only in his notes.

That gap is compounded by an address the customer explicitly flagged as unresolved: 'I have what I fully believe it is, I think it will be best to make sure that we confirm,' then 'it might be 2090 Woodward Street. Hold on,' then 'I will reach back out to triple confirm but they have like, yeah, it, there's some mixed messaging here.' Two candidate pickup addresses, the customer openly uncertain, and no written record for her to correct and no stated owner of the follow-up.

No deposit was never explicitly stated. The customer asked a direct payment-anxiety question — 'what is the minimum that I have to pay for Friday?' — and got a good answer on billing mechanics ('it's not like you have to like, pay it upfront and then you get rebated') but never the clean 'there's no deposit to book' line.

No hours and no direct number given — 'you're more than welcome to reach out to me. My name is Hector, I'm the operations manager for the south Austin branch' names the person without giving her any way to reach him.

Customer's name was never used once. Not in the greeting, not during the pricing, not in the farewell — sixteen and a half minutes, an unusually personal conversation about her pregnancy, and zero name use.
top_strength: Hector solved a genuinely hard scheduling problem that most reps would have either refused or crammed onto one day, and he solved it in the customer's favor. She raised a third stop mid-call — a furniture pickup at the Four Hands warehouse that needed to land at the new house — and instead of bolting it onto an already six-hour Saturday, he thought out loud about what that would actually do to her: 'I'm just trying to work out some logistics here to make sure that we don't have a too late of an evening for you with that additional stop... I'm a little, wanna be a little bit cautious just to make sure that we're not having too late of the evening and finishing I'd say, you know, 89 o'clock in the evening.' Then he proposed the split: 'do you have availability on Friday to that end? We can kind of pick up from the warehouse location and then drop it off at Norwood' — and explained why it was better for her, not just easier for the branch: 'the crew that does your move on Saturday they will have a little bit more time to actually take care of the reassembly or the assembly in general for you.' She took it instantly. He then proactively checked the new stop against the service zone before she could worry about it — 'Just wanted to double-check and make sure that was within our free travel zone. And with how close it is to our branch, like, no worries there... You shouldn't have to worry about any [trip] fees' — and stayed calm when she produced two different possible warehouse addresses. The best moment on the call is the one that cost the branch money. When she said 'I just don't think we're gonna hit that minimum with the job. It's like smaller,' he did not defend the policy and did not upsell. He fixed it: 'I might be able let, I'll go ahead and reduce the minimum we can do that for a special cases in that to where I can get it down to two hours at that rate.' That took the Friday job from $555 to $444, unprompted, and it is why she ended the call saying 'thank you so much Hector I really appreciate it.' He also ran the arithmetic cleanly and stated all three numbers — $444 day one, $1,332 day two, $1,776 total — which is more transparency than most of this week's sample offered.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Hector restructured this customer's entire move and then sent her nothing. Two bookings, two changed start times, a reduced minimum, a reassigned assembly crew, a $1,776 total, and a pickup address she herself said twice she could not confirm — none of it in writing. That is the biggest single risk in this week's batch. The close needed to be: 'Amanda, I'm sending you a confirmation right now with all of it bolded at the top — Friday the 18th at 2:30 for the Four Hands pickup at a two-hour minimum, Saturday the 19th at 12:30 for the house, $444 and $1,332, $1,776 together. The warehouse address is the one piece we're not sure on, so once your rep confirms it, reply to that email with the right one and I'll update it.' That fixes the email handoff, the bolded list, the verification ask, and it assigns an owner to the loose address instead of leaving it floating between two people. Second priority: the probe came in at 3/9 on a sixteen-minute call, which is the real story here. No box count, no stairs at either end, no access questions at any of three stops, no walk distances, no packing offer. Hector inherited Arden's six-hour estimate and never rebuilt it — even after learning three separate things that should have moved it: the house is roughly 1,000 square feet not 1,200, a chunk of the contents is already sitting in the new garage, and the Four Hands stop was lifted off Saturday entirely onto Friday. Three downward pressures and the number did not move an inch. Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-4 review: he also said the padding out loud — 'what we tried to do with the estimate is lean more so on the conservative side, in an effort to avoid surprises.' That sentence is the habit Cameron's third expectation is aimed at, and it is being delivered to customers as a feature. Conservative is not free: it inflates the quote, it sets a soft bar the crew has no pressure to beat, and it is the mechanism behind the 45-46% number. Pull the actual against this one — a 1,000-square-foot three-bedroom, partially pre-moved, with the warehouse stop removed, is a strong candidate to land well under six hours. Third, the differentiators: 8/20 on pricing with no what's-included list, no No Worries, no Meet Your Mover, no On-Time Guarantee. The pregnancy and the two-crew structure make Meet Your Mover almost self-writing here, and brand-new furniture moving from a manufacturer's warehouse makes No Worries the obvious one. Finally, on presence: Hector's rapport is real and it is the best thing about this call — the 'how's your morning going,' the congratulations, the reduced minimum — but he never used her name once, and warmth without discovery is what produced a 3/9 probe on a sixteen-minute call. The fix is not less warmth, it is spending the rapport on questions: 'With the baby coming and the bathrooms still being worked on, tell me what's going to be in the way on move day' gets the access constraint and the stressor answer at the same time.
phone_presence_notes: Genuinely warm and personally invested — he asked 'How's your morning going so far?' mid-call, responded to the pregnancy with real enthusiasm ('Wow, congratulations... I'm glad that we're helping you get everything settled and you don't have to shoulder everything yourself'), answered her question back about his own day honestly, and then backed the warmth with an actual concession by cutting her minimum unprompted; held at 4 rather than 5 because he never used her name once in sixteen minutes and the delivery carries a heavy 'is like' filler tic that makes several explanations hard to follow.
audio_review_reason: The clarity-and-pace bullet was deducted on transcript evidence that is hard to separate from transcription artifact. Sentences repeatedly render as run-ons anchored on a filler phrase — 'is like we'll be happy to help out in that regard is like it just, again in that regard is just gonna be a little bit additional time' — and the hourly rate itself comes through garbled as 'that'll equate to an hourly rate of $200 $22.' Audio is needed to tell whether the customer actually heard a clean $222 and a coherent explanation, or whether the delivery is as circuitous as it reads.
